Senses.Explanation: Long rain without clearing names persistent wet weather and supplies a repeatable image in hall discourse. Yunmen Wenyan uses it as a reply about his house style; Xuedou Chongxian and Dahui Zonggao speak from changes in the weather; Liao’an Yu contrasts soaked monks with drought-stricken farmers; Yuan’an Liao intensifies the storm image; and Qizong Zhen answers a quoted rain saying in his own voice.

AlternateTargets: The vital matter stayed long unspoken; he did not rush to tell it.

Senses.Note: Ruibai turns the familiar pair toward what he reveals at a tea gathering. Shending Yikui makes the delay end with an immediate presentation at a funeral, Tianze joins silence and speech in a new sermon, and Lingji uses it at a coffin rite. The phrase is inherited wording, but each selected teacher voices it in a fresh present turn rather than transporting an old case dialogue.

Senses.Note: The line opens a four-part scriptural instruction that also says not to extinguish deluded mind, not to add knowing to its objects, and not to divide the real within absence of knowing. Juelang interleaves ordinary hunger and cold, then asks whether his gloss fits the scripture. Daxiu relates the passage to a verse, Hanyue reads the four clauses as one, and Pufu answers with a terse comment. Beijian and Shuzhong supply separate verses. In each cited span the exact line remains the Buddha's, while the named teachers interpret it.

Senses.Explanation: The scriptural pair calls for no deluded thought in every circumstance. Its later clauses also reject forcibly extinguishing delusion and adding a second layer of knowing. Recorded sayings turn the pair toward everyday hunger, ordinary actions, and verses about change.

Senses.PreferredTarget: At every moment, do not raise delusive thoughts; do not try to extinguish the delusive mind
AlternateTargets: Do not give rise to false thoughts at any time, yet do not suppress the thoughts already present
SearchAliases: do not raise thoughts do not extinguish delusive mind
Perfect Enlightenment Sutra thoughts not suppress
Senses.Note: In the Perfect Enlightenment scripture, the pair continues: do not add knowing to a delusive object, and do not distinguish a supposed truth in that non-knowing. Azi warns against mistaking it for a still inner light, Dawei demands more than a verbal reading, Miyun asks where the Buddha works now, Wanru answers with a tiger and a staff, Buhui gives a seasonal verse, and Wuyi asks whether the four negatives kill or bring life. The exact scripture wording is attributed to Shakyamuni Buddha; each later master provides a distinct current application.

Senses.Explanation: When the lion roars, green grass springs up; when the elephant king looks back, flowers fall red. The paired animal images present living authority as immediate and transformative. Current deployments include Juelang Daosheng in J25nB174, Linye Tongqi in J26nB186, Eryin Mi in J28nB212, Hanyu Hongxian in J33nB288, and Huiyue Xu in J38nB418. The full paired image remains the lexical unit. The color and motion are poetic effects, not a literal zoological description.

Senses.Explanation: The lion teaches its cub by bewildering it: as the cub prepares to spring forward, the verse says it has already turned over. Wumen Huikai attaches the line to Yunmen's blows for Dongshan. Tiantong Rujing pairs the same line with grandmotherly concern that does not deceive, while Hansong Zhicao uses it in a father-and-son exchange where Huanglong's invitation and Longqing's counter expose one another. Mi’an Xianjie quotes the complete verse as an old saying; his occurrence does not identify Dongshan. The image names demanding instruction through the cub's bewilderment and sudden turn.

Senses.Explanation: The Chan records quote the formula (驅耕夫之牛, driving off the plowman's ox) as the first half of the pair they reach for when a guide takes away what the person in front of them is leaning on: drive off the plowman's ox and snatch the hungry man's food. Masters state it as the test of who may stand as a guide — Wuzu Fayan and Dongshan Shouchu define the good guide by it, and Tianyi Huai speaks it as his precept only to decline it in the same breath — while Yuanwu Keqin, Hongzhi Zhengjue, Poshan Haiming, and Tianyin Yuanxiu fold it into commentary, verse, and their own turns. Wuzu Fayan ascends the hall and raises what the ancients said: one who serves as a good guide must drive off the plowman's ox and snatch the hungry man's food. He then presses the formula's own double edge in his own voice — if you drive off the ox, why do the crops flourish; if you snatch the food, why does hunger end for good — and adds that only someone with the pair's hands and feet can corner a student with it. Dongshan Shouchu turns the same standard into a definition: a good guide is one who drives off the plowman's ox and snatches the hungry man's food, and which of today's crowd is a real one. Tianyi Huai speaks the formula as his own precept — one who serves as lineage teacher must drive off the plowman's ox and snatch the hungry man's food — and then declines both halves before the same assembly: he will not drive the ox off, he will not snatch the food; what use has he for the ox, what would he eat of the food. His address survives in eight independent corpus containers - two retained here - and the imperially selected record files it under his name. Yuanwu Keqin writes to a student that from the ancients onward the stick and the shout, each device and each word, have aimed at complete release alone — what is called driving off the plowman's ox and snatching the hungry man's food — and that whoever cannot work this way is a mud-ball man. At the funeral fire of Foyan Qingyuan — his fellow heir under Wuzu Fayan — he gives the pair a reading in terms of inherited tools: the chestnut burr Foyan made use of all his life drives off the ox, and the diamond ring entrusted in Yangqi's line snatches the food. Case commentary uses the pair as the measure of an old master's move. Yuanwu holds that only someone with the pair's hands and feet sees where Mazu stood for people in his sickbed answer; praising Xinghua's blow he calls it good ox-driving and food-snatching; and Sixin Wuxin, appraising the Longya exchange, grants that Longya drove off the ox and snatched the food, yet still asks where the meaning of the founder's coming from the west is in that. Hongzhi Zhengjue works the pair from both sides. On the Muzhou case he grants that with this driving and snatching a lineage teacher's means are present, adding that Tiantong cannot help following with praise; on the Bajiao case he withholds it — Bajiao knew good from bad yet could not drive off the ox or snatch the food, and were someone to ask Hongzhi himself, he says, he would simply strike along with the sound. Later masters fold the pair into their own turns. Poshan Haiming splits it across silence and speech — in silence he speaks and drives off the ox, in speaking he is silent and snatches the food, a tongue that talks without talking — and asks the assembly who this is. Tianyin Yuanxiu, defending the direct Linji line against rivals who stamp people with a fixed seal, runs the pair in reverse order — snatch the food, drive off the ox — and asks when it ever bound anyone with real dharmas. The pair rides Linji Yixuan's four alternatives. The instruction lists the ways he works — illumination before function, function before illumination, both at once, both apart — and at simultaneous illumination-and-function it places the pair, with marrow-drilling and needle-sharp pricks beside it. The received T-canon Linji record carries no such passage, but the received line is not the instruction's only corpus carrier: a Linji section of the Jiaxing canon carries it verbatim (照用同時，驅耕夫之牛，奪饑人之食), the supplementary record of Linji Huizhao carries it with the first verb in a variant graph, and the imperially selected record preserves it in Linji's own voice; later masters quote it under his name — Chuiwan has the old man Linji say it when he presses what one who has awakened must still pass through.

Occurrences.Kwic: 新好，而以組綉作佛事。一一針孔一世界，一一花葉一如來，森羅萬象影重重，莫不一法之所印。此座非高亦非廣，此被非闊亦非狹，舒即大千悉彌滿，收入微塵不迫窄。譬如隨色摩尼珠，是被光明亦如是，晝夜常轉如是輪，須彌燈王為作證。佛成道，上堂：雪山六年覰不破，七處九會說不到。合水和泥，招因帶果。殊不知衲僧門下，北斗東轉，南斗西移。上堂：拶得行時，方知玄路絕。智不到處，道著頭角生。縱使驅耕夫牛，奪飢人食，別有生涯，猶是不著。便不見道，纔有一絲頭，便有一絲頭。聖節，上堂。河清海晏，含有象於不言；天成地平，謝無私於何處？靈山蘊界不居，萬緣不涉，只於出入息間供養承事無量壽世尊而作佛事。且道是知恩耶？報恩耶？元宵，謝新首座兼開平西堂赴東山，上堂。燃無盡燈，示無盡意，藕絲竅裡逗須彌，蟭螟眼中放夜市。一等是舊話重行，且道是多子塔前、險崖句裏？良久，云：東山下，左邊底。上堂：始從

Occurrences.Kwic: 無餘聲色可呈君，箇中若了全無事，體用無妨分不分。鵶鳴鵲噪，法法圓成；水淥山青，頭頭顯煥。見亦同見，聞亦同聞，因什麼有迷有悟？良久，云：莫言佛法無多子，不是苦心人不知。上堂，云：若是知有底人，入林不動草，入水不動波，便能脫珍御服，掛弊垢衣，與眾魔共一手，作諸勞侶，接待方來，猶是傍借邊事。何也？澄源湛水尚棹孤舟，古佛道場猶乘車子。若是箇中人，直須向虵頭上揩痒，驪頷下抉珠，驅耕夫牛，奪飢人食。若能如是，始解坐報化佛頭，踏盧遮那頂。法昌與麼說話，大似夢中說夢。何謂也？爭似不來還不往，亦無懽笑亦無愁。上堂，僧問：佛佛授手，祖祖相傳，未審傳箇什麼？師云：須彌頂上鐵崑崙。進云：當表何事？師云：去國知歸路，伶俜獲寶珠。進云：實際理地，不受一塵，未審珠向什麼處安者？師云：從來光璨爛，不用強安排。進云：與麼則謝師指示。師云：珠在什麼處？僧擬議，師云：了。師乃云：見聞如

Senses.Explanation: Drive off the ploughmans ox and snatch food from a hungry person is a forceful image for stripping away what a student relies on. Yuanwu, Xiaoyin, Yanxi, and Fachang use it in independent present instruction; one useful lamp context remains. Yanxi says even this severe intervention falls short, while Fachang tests and then undercuts his own formulation. Retained public meaning is supported by independent present uses in recorded discourse.
